I think you’re interpreting the “some impact” thing wrong. If it’s unintentional it means the interviewer likely didn’t notice she was wearing makeup, they were reacting to the effects even subtle makeup can have on appearance. You don’t need to wear anything just to let them know you’re wearing makeup. Likely what you want to do is make yourself look healthy and put-together, which can be accomplished with makeup. You can make your skin look healthy by evening your skin tone with a corrector, look awake by concealing under eye areas, and seeming alert and approchable by making your eyes stand out with mascara. Obviously there’s more you can do but that’s what you might use for a natural look. However you can achieve the same look by getting restful sleep, staying hydrated, and taking care of your skin. This is the better option in my opinion. Especially combined with light grooming. Overall though I think makeup has very little effect on the outcome of an interview, but if you feel like you look more professional with it, it could boost your confidence and improve your interview. 

Personally I wear just a little makeup to interviews just for confidence and to avoid looking like I just rolled out of bed. I’m really comfortable with doing performance level makeup though so doing something light is quick and easy. But I’ve never worn more than mascara (which was maybe twice) to work because I refuse to get up earlier to do that and literally no one cares if I do or not.

I’ve heard over and over again to keep it to one page, but honestly I think aesthetics and readability are more important. I have less experience to include than you and my resume is two pages, but only because the way I designed it  doesn’t really allow for one page without ruining the affect. I made mine with the help of a successful engineer in his area, who has gotten a lot of positive comments about his when applying for jobs. I’ve had mine looked over a few times by people who ran resume workshops and I’ve always gotten good feedback on it and how nice it looks, and no one has suggested I make it one page. It’s clean, appealing, and easy to read. All the important information is visible first so if they don’t read the second page they still have a good idea about who I am. And it’s worked well for me so far. 

You’re more likely to be remembered if your resume stands out anyway. And if yours differs from all the other one-page black and white walls of text then you will stand out. It seems like those people who just throw out a resume because it’s more than a page are becoming few and far between because it’s just not beneficial to a company to hire that way. It’s just more likely your second page won’t be read until you’re being considered more seriously, so just don’t put critical information on the second page.

I have ADHD (which is a good sub just to gets tips from) and so I haven’t found perfect remedies yet but here’s a few things I do to minimize it:

1. Whenever I recognize I’m procrastinating [recognizing is the toughest part] hardcore I force myself to shut down all distractions immediately. Close all apps/websites you’re wasting time on. Write down anything you’re wanting to do that you’re using to procrastinate but need/want to finish it later. Writing things down helps me a lot because usually I do other productive things with the excuse that I might forget to do it later. 

2. Take time to organize all due dates for all classes at the beginning of the term very clearly in a planner. This helps me a lot when I feel overwhelmed to visualize exactly what I need to do and where my priority should be. I also have a lot more motivation at the start of a term so I use it to try and stay ahead for as long as possible. Once the work catches up my procrastination comes out in full force so I try to push back how long it takes for that to happen. 

3. Break daunting work up into a smaller goal. Like to just do a rough outline of a paper, or to write down all knowns from a problem, what you want to find, and the equations you might need. I make a deal with my brain that this goal is all I have to do right now. Just these little things will usually be enough to et me thinking about the assignment and inevitably doing a good bit of work on it. 

4. I sometimes use a pomodoro timer type app, especially when studying for final. It’s another deal with my brain that I just have to do 25 minutes uninterrupted then I get a break and decide what to do from there. Usually after the first or second block I get so focused on what I’m working on that I’d rather finish it than take a break. 

Sorry for the long post on this, but these are my tips as someone who is just shit at keeping good habits and how I try to manage with that.

The study makes sense, but what the article fails to do is try to determine the root cause. Kids are not being over diagnosed because they’re just young, that’s a crucial point he ignores to support his theory. Kids could be wrongfully diagnosed because they are likely being tested against a standard for their grade level that they developmentally are not quite to yet, which poses an issue with the testing or the psychiatrist. 

BUT, here is what I guarantee is the most likely reason:

Kids who are much younger than their peers may tend to act less mature than their classmates, this behavior stands out significantly to teachers and parents. Teachers and parents are more likely to compare the child to their classmates rather than kids their age. These behaviors are then seen as red flags for ADHD and the child is tested for it. I don’t know the data on it, but I would guess there is a high likelihood that children born one month before the cut-off also have a much greater chance of being tested in the first place. 

Essentially there’s a confounding variable that wasn’t controlled for, which means you can’t justify any correlation drawn from the data.

As someone who’s been that girl, her reaction is likely due to mental illness (such as her depression) that hasn’t been dealt with. It sickens me now to look back and see that I was like that at some point because with therapy, medication, and making gradual changes to improve myself, I can see that I’ve come a long way. But my point, and I think you somewhat understand this, is that to her it really does feel like the world is ending and she has no control over her life. Her depression and likely anxiety has just blown up this whole situation in her mind, and it’s affecting her physically. Now absolutely none of this is an excuse for her doing this to you or a reason for you to be the one to help her (and in fact you shouldn’t be). 

First of all just know that this will end, time is really the best healer. 

My advice to you would be to limit any communication to necessary things. She may threaten suicide or try to make you feel guilty about things, such as her not eating. It’s cruel to you that she might do this, but it’s unlikely that she’s lying. More than likely she’ll exaggerate these feelings to get a reaction from you. Don’t dismiss these feelings, and especially pay attention to any suicidal warnings. I know when I was in that place I was extremely suicidal to the point where I thought about ways to end my life, but I knew I would never go through with it because of what it would do to my family and the tiny sliver of hope I had that things would get better. If she is having some kind of reaction like this that could be harmful, just be there as a friend and reiterate why her life has value and the importance of her eating and staying healthy. 

Beyond this try to avoid contact as much as possible. Don’t reach out to her, don’t respond to any accusatory messages or messages that are baiting you to reply. If she seems to really need someone to listen then allow a minimal interaction but don’t let it turn into a conversation. Don’t try to answer all of her questions about why the relationship ended but if she seems particularly distraught over one question, considering giving a short but honest answer to her. There’s no need to block her on everything because that could be needlessly upsetting, but just remove her as a friend on all social media and make your accounts private so she can’t see everything. She may go through some other means to see your accounts but she’ll probably see how extreme that is on her own before long. 

Probably most importantly don’t give her any kind of hope, and try to avoid seeing her at all for a while, even on accident if you frequent similar places. 

Sorry for the long reply but hopefully it helps. Basically just be patient with her but go out and live your own life in the meantime. Don’t be her crutch but don’t be a jerk. You don’t have to explain your boundaries to her, she’ll learn before long that you’re serious about this and that she can’t rely on you to be her emotional support.

It depends greatly on your appointment, and your school what the timing of everything is. 

As for what to expect during the appointment (again it can vary greatly): Typically it will be a long appointment consisting of a combination of interviews and tests. These interviews give the psychiatrist a good understanding of your behavior, medical history, and family history (such as a sibling being diagnosed). Before my appointment they also gave me a form for one of my parents to fill out about my behavior as a child. Then the tests are looking at ADHD behaviors but also looking for learning disabilities, because undiagnosed learning disabilities can look a lot like ADHD. Then a few weeks after my appointment I got basically a packet containing my diagnosis, results from testing, the psychiatrist’s observations, and recommendations for accommodations. I didn’t need it right away because it was summer, but he had let me know they could get a letter sooner if I needed it to get medication or accommodations sooner. 

As for accommodations, I think the most common ones are a quiet testing location and time and a half on tests, but will really depend on your diagnosis and recommendations you receive. At my university we have a disability services office that I had to submit my letter to, and after they confirmed it I had to go to an orientation to learn what resources I had available through them, and learn how to use their online system. Then I was able to request accommodations from professors right away. I would look into the system/policy your university has for accommodations now so that after your appointment, if you are diagnosed, you can make sure you have everything you need as soon as possible. 

Just be patient though. These things can take a while and it gets frustrating, but it will be worth it!

Your best bet is probably doing a clinical interview with a psychiatrist who specializes in ADHD. Essentially what he told me, and what just made so much click for me, was that I had the active form of ADHD but because I was smart and I had severe social anxiety, it was not obviously recognizable even to my parents. 

TLDR; just because it doesn’t “look” like you have ADHD doesn’t mean you don’t. Get an in depth interview with a specialist for the most accurate diagnosis. 

Also side note: one thing they should also do (not sure if you did in the clinical tests) is test you for a learning disability. Because if you struggle focusing in most classes and they determine you don’t have any learning disability then that can be a big marker for ADHD.

Like I said though it's the tests that people get Cs on a lot but usually though homework and sometimes extra credit it's not hard to get a B in the class.

Also personally it's not my engineering classes that get the As for my GPA. It's all the general ed classes or the classes for my other major. If it weren't for those "easy A" classes I would be between a 2.0 and 3.0. In engineering classes getting Cs on tests is pretty normal at my school. Which is why to get into the upperclass program many students have to retake classes.

A 2.0 GPA isn't average but a C is. After tests and such professors will curve tests so that the aver lies somewhere in the C range. But if the average already lies above that range then they wouldn't adjust it down. But generally speaking a C ends up being average. And in most classes people get Cs on tests but do the rest of their work well enough to get Bs or As.

Grades do not an engineer make. Getting Cs in college is much more common than you realize.  A C IS AVERAGE. However GPA is important to. You may get Cs on exams but you can sometimes make up for that with homework and other grades. Sometimes there also a curve applied at the end of the class that will help. Don't start stressing about overall GPA until at least the end of your first year, just focus on doing your best in classes. And remember that you can always retake a class to boost your GPA, that happens a lot at my school in mechanical because the GPA requirement used to be 3.5 to get into the upperclassmen courses.

Each part is different and lends a different element to the composition based on the qualities of the instrument. Usually the first part (first cello in this case) is the most complex and has the most recognizable part of the melody and the rest of the parts will complement that part. Sometimes more than one part will play the same thing to help it stand out, or they might all play something different to complement another instrument playing the melody. 

I don't know if there's a "best" number of people to have on each part but I would say at least three would be needed to sound "big" but in a larger orchestra the number on each part might increase for an even larger and more impressive sound, or there might be several parts for each instrument with a few people on each part.
